```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_eipack <- requireNamespace("eiPack", quietly = TRUE)
```

Version 0.2.0 adds `eiBounds()`, which extends the 2 x 2 method of Jiang,
King, Schmaltz and Tanner (2019) to R x C tables, to units nested in groups
(e.g. polls within ridings, precincts within counties), and to a ladder of
assumptions running from Duncan–Davis bounds (no model) to Goodman constancy.
The derivations, proofs and simulations are in `docs/extension/` of the source
repository. `PLAIN_LANGUAGE_GUIDE.md` there explains every rung in plain terms.

## What is reported

For each target (by default every row-by-column cell), `eiBounds()` reports:

* `estimate`: the estimated identified set for the *model-implied rate*. This
  is not a confidence interval, and it tends to be too narrow when there are
  many noisy constraints.
* `ci_model`: a confidence interval for the model-implied rate at the observed
  compositions (the "behavioural" rate).
* `ci_actual`: a confidence interval for the *actual* rate in these units.
  It includes an allowance for unit-level deviations, which can never be
  estimated. That allowance is bounded by the Bhatia–Davis inequality (the
  default) or by the Popoviciu bound of 1/4 used by Jiang et al.
* `duncan_davis`: the model-free bounds for the actual rate.

The confidence intervals use intersection-bound inference (Chernozhukov, Lee
and Rosen 2013). Jiang et al.'s CI_x intervals are also available
(`jkst = TRUE`).

## Two-by-two: the original method

```{r census}
library(eiPartialID)
library(eco)
data(census)
fit <- eiBounds(x = census$X, t = census$Y, n = census$N, model = "M0",
                targets = list(black_literate = c(1, 1)), jkst = TRUE, seed = 1)
fit
```

With `range_offset = 1e-5` and `vcov = "HC1"`, the plug-in bound and the
CI_x intervals coincide with `generateBounds()` and `evaluateBounds()`.

## Three ways to give the data

```{r interfaces, eval = has_eipack}
library(eiPack)
data(senc)                       # NC registration by race, with true cell counts
senc2 <- transform(senc, black = black + natam)   # merge a very small group
# 1. formula with counts
f1 <- eiBounds(cbind(dem, rep, non) ~ cbind(white, black), data = senc2,
               targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")), seed = 1)
# 2. data plus column names
f2 <- eiBounds(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"), cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"),
               targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")), seed = 1)
# 3. shares and sizes
X <- as.matrix(senc2[, c("white", "black")]) / senc2$total
T <- as.matrix(senc2[, c("dem", "rep", "non")]) / senc2$total
f3 <- eiBounds(x = X, t = T, n = senc2$total, targets = list(white_dem = c(1, 1)), seed = 1)
rbind(f1$table$estimate_lower, f2$table$estimate_lower, f3$table$estimate_lower)
```

Row and column totals must describe the same population. If they differ,
`eiBounds()` stops; `mismatch = "rescale"` overrides this, with a warning.

## The ladder

`ladder()` runs the rungs from the most to the least plausible:

| Rung | Assumption |
|---|---|
| DD | none |
| M2 | each group has its own linear contextual effects |
| M1(delta) | contextual effects shared, each group within `delta` of them |
| M1 | contextual effects shared; groups differ only in baselines ("group dummies") |
| L4 | as M1, and one chosen row has no contextual effect |
| L5 | constancy within each group (Goodman within groups) |
| L6 | Goodman constancy |

M0 (pooled, no groups) is reported alongside; it is not nested with the others.

```{r ladder, eval = has_eipack}
L <- ladder(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"), cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"),
            group = "county", targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")),
            row_constant = "black")
L
# truth
with(senc, sum(whdem) / sum(white))
```

## Composition range

The bounds come from requiring the implied rates to be valid probabilities at
the corners of the composition range. The choices are:

* `range = "hull"` (default): the observed units. Each group uses its own units.
* `range = "trim"`: drop extreme units from the corners (`trim = list(quantile
  = 0.01)`, `min_n = ...` or `drop = ...`). Trimmed units enter the actual rate
  only through their Duncan–Davis bounds, so trimming never relies on the model
  for them.
* `range = "extrapolate"`: impose the model beyond the data (`"simplex"` means
  pure units). This gives narrower bounds, but it is untestable, and a warning is
  printed.

## Additional restrictions

All of these keep the bounds as linear programs.

```{r restrictions, eval = has_eipack}
r <- list(
  order = list(c(high = "black", low = "white", col = "dem")),  # same composition: black >= white
  sign = list(list(row = "white", col = "dem", from = "white", to = "black", sign = 1)),
  slope = 0.5,                                                  # no rate moves > 0.5 across compositions
  external = list(list(target = c("white", "dem"), lower = 0.40, upper = 0.55))  # e.g. a survey
)
eiBounds(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"), cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"),
         targets = list(white_dem = c("white", "dem")), restrictions = r, seed = 1)
```

`zeros` fixes structural zeros, e.g. a party that did not run. `linear` takes
any linear restriction on the contextual-effect matrices.

## Signs on associations and contextual reinforcement

Two kinds of "monotone EI" belief (Elzayn et al., *Monotone Ecological
Inference*) can be added to the linear-contextual-effects rungs as extra rows:

* the **between** association $\delta_B$: within the same unit, group $r$ is
  on average more (or less) likely than the rest to choose column $c$;
* the **within** (contextual) association $\delta_W$: group rates rise (or
  fall) on average with the group's own share of the unit;
* **contextual reinforcement (CR)**: $\delta_B$ and $\delta_W$ have the same
  sign, without saying which.

All three are model-implied means with design weights $N_i$. A sign is one
linear row; CR is a union of two branches. With the one-vs-rest version (`"W1"`,
the default, and every 2 x 2 table) CR is a single slab
$D^r \in [\gamma_r ER^r, ER^r]$, so it stays one LP. The other pairings (`"W2"`,
`"pair"`) can give **two disjoint intervals**; they are printed as
`[a, b] U [c, d]` (use `union = "hull"` for the hull).

```{r sign}
set.seed(2)
n <- 200
x <- pmin(pmax(rbeta(n, 2, 2) * 0.8 + 0.1, 0.02), 0.98)
m0 <- 0.40 + 0.20 * x; m1 <- 0.55 + 0.05 * x          # linear means, CR holds
t <- (1 - x) * rbeta(n, m0 * 15, (1 - m0) * 15) + x * rbeta(n, m1 * 15, (1 - m1) * 15)
N <- sample(300:3000, n, replace = TRUE)
gap <- list(gap = matrix(c(1, -1, 0, 0), 2, 2))      # B(X -> T) - B(notX -> T)
jkst <- eiBounds(x = x, t = t, n = N, targets = gap, seed = 1)   # linear rung alone
jkst$table[, c("estimate_lower", "estimate_upper", "ci_model_lower", "ci_model_upper")]
cr <- eiBounds(x = x, t = t, n = N, targets = gap, seed = 1,
               restrictions = list(cr = list(list(row = 1, col = 1))))
cr
dW <- eiBounds(x = x, t = t, n = N, targets = gap, seed = 1,
               restrictions = list(assoc = list(list(type = "dW", row = 1, col = 1, sign = 1))))
dW$table[, c("estimate_lower", "estimate_upper", "ci_model_lower", "ci_model_upper")]
```

`eiRedundancy()` (stored in `$sign` when sign or CR restrictions are given)
reports, for each restriction and target, whether it is already implied by the
data and the rung, cuts the set but not this quantity, or narrows this
quantity, with the gain when added first and when added last. The verdict uses
a face test (one LP per endpoint), never solver dual values. It also shows the
associations' intervals under the rung alone and the EGGHM quantities
$\widehat{ER}$, $\widehat{NM} = \gamma\widehat{ER}$ and $\gamma$:

```{r sign2}
cr$sign$descriptive
cr$sign$verdicts[, c("restriction", "verdict_first", "gain_first")]
```

How to read and report these:

* **The estimate is sharp for the regression.** Under the linear rung plus
  sign rows, the LP interval is exactly the set of values consistent with the
  fitted regression and the beliefs (PHASE5a R3).
* **What the data can and cannot check.** A sign on $\delta_W$ can be refuted
  by aggregate data. With two groups, a sign on $\delta_B$ and CR can never be
  refuted by aggregates on their own: an empty set refutes their combination
  with the linear rung, and messages name the whole combination. Their
  credibility rests on substantive argument or individual-level data.
* **They can buy a lot.** In the PHASE5a Monte Carlo (2 x 2, truth on the CR
  edge) the CR interval had median width 0.36 against 1.1 for the linear rung
  alone, with coverage 0.99.
* **Never intersect the estimated bracket $[\gamma\widehat{ER}, \widehat{ER}]$
  with a confidence interval.** Treating the estimated bracket as known
  under-covers (about 0.90 at the CR edge, and it does not improve with $n$).
  The package inflates every piece instead: the conservative CI inflates each
  piece of the slab before taking the maximum; the CLR CI (default) takes the
  union of the two branch CIs, each at the full level.
* Our $\widehat{ER}$ uses the fitted $E[T \mid X]$; it equals the EGGHM
  $T$-based $\widehat{ER}$ when `weights = "n"`.

`ladder()` takes sign and CR rungs through `sign_rungs`, e.g.
`sign_rungs = list("M0 + CR" = list(restrictions = list(cr = list(list(row = 1, col = 1)))))`.

## Sensitivity and breakdown

```{r sens}
sv <- sensitivity(fit, eta = c(0, 0.02, 0.05))
sv[, c("eta", "estimate_lower", "estimate_upper")]
breakdown(fit, "black_literate", threshold = 0.5, which = "ci_model")
```

`eta` is how far average rates may depart from straight lines, in probability
units, in ways the data cannot detect. The breakdown value is the largest
`eta` at which the conclusion ("the rate is above 0.5") still holds.

## Benchmarks

`eiBenchmark()` runs the rungs on datasets with known cell counts, and reports
whether each interval contains the truth and how wide it is.

```{r bench, eval = has_eipack}
truth <- with(senc, matrix(c(sum(whdem), sum(whrep), sum(whnon),
                             sum(bldem + natamdem), sum(blrep + natamrep), sum(blnon + natamnon)),
                           2, 3, byrow = TRUE))
b <- eiBenchmark(list(senc = list(data = senc2, rows = c("white", "black"),
                                  cols = c("dem", "rep", "non"), group = "county", truth = truth)),
                 rungs = c("M0", "M1", "L5"), seed = 1)
aggregate(cbind(in_ci_actual, width_ci_actual, width_dd) ~ rung, b, mean)
```

### Real elections with known truth: ei.Datasets

`eiDatasetsTables()` builds 492 tables with exact truth from the New Zealand
general elections 2002–2020 in the `ei.Datasets` package. In each electorate,
polling places are the units, party votes are the rows and electorate
(candidate) votes are the columns. The repository's
`benchmarks/run_ei_datasets_benchmark.R` runs the full benchmark, and the
results are stored in `benchmarks/results/`.

```{r eidatasets, eval = FALSE}
tb <- eiDatasetsTables(elections = 2020)
eiBenchmark(tb[1:5], rungs = c("M0", "L6"), seed = 1)
```
